video_notes.title: McKinsey Presentation Slide Review: Consulting Slide Review From Former Bain & Company Consultant
video_notes.contributed: A single-slide teardown of a real McKinsey exhibit that turns four review lenses (title/message, structure, evidence, formatting) into a repeatable checklist for critiquing your own slides.

video_notes.title: Consulting Presentation Tips from former McKinsey Consultant
video_notes.contributed: Reviews six audience-submitted decks live, surfacing a wider catalog of concrete slide-writing fixes (font consistency, action titles, dewording, alignment/jitter, animation, banking vs. consulting norms) than a single-slide teardown can show.

video_notes.title: A Meta Engineer's Agentic Engineering Workflow
video_notes.contributed: Not a presentation-design talk — it's a coding-agent workflow demo — but it documents a concrete pattern for communicating status/insights to a person juggling many concurrent threads: recap-first updates, one question at a time, plain language, an explicit next action, and evidence (screenshots, risk assessment) attached to a report instead of raw claims.

claims.claim: Before designing any slide, do the analysis needed to know the one message you want to communicate — an unclear message produces an unclear slide.
claims.quote: the title and the message is so important

claims.claim: Slides fail most often because the author skipped the work of distilling data into a single clear takeaway before building the visual.
claims.quote: you need to collect the data do the analysis and then you know the message

claims.claim: A strong title is one line, states exactly what to take away, and prioritizes only the most important points rather than listing everything.
claims.quote: it's one line it's not too long it clearly states

claims.claim: When trends or facts differ in importance, say so explicitly in the title — pick the ones that matter instead of presenting them as equal.
claims.quote: they focusing on on the key ones

claims.claim: A title that only describes the topic ("five major trends") without naming the standout insight (which trend matters most) is merely descriptive, not insightful — push for a point of view.
claims.quote: it's a tad descriptive i think it's it's insightful but it doesn't it doesn't put out a point of view

claims.claim: Keep slide structure simple — a small number of clearly divided zones (e.g., labels on the left, data on the right) beats a complex layout meant to impress.
claims.quote: it's a simple slide which which i love

claims.claim: Don't give a chart legend its own column — move it to the bottom so it doesn't eat space that should go to content.
claims.quote: i think we they could have moved it down

claims.claim: Back claims with visible data in a simplified chart rather than bare assertions — it adds credibility even without commentary.
claims.quote: it's always strong when your slides are full of data

claims.claim: Note where a data point or assessment came from (interviews, surveys, expert judgment) directly on the slide — omitting a source line undercuts credibility.
claims.quote: i would have liked in the source some notes how they got to these numbers

claims.claim: Create visual hierarchy primarily through font size (largest for the title, next for section labels, smallest for detail) instead of boxes or extra chrome.
claims.quote: they use primarily the size of the text to to show hierarchy

claims.claim: Use connector lines to make the relationship between a label and its data point explicit rather than leaving readers to infer it.
claims.quote: these little lines here to to clearly make the connection between the trend and the impact

claims.claim: Keep every row/element aligned to the same grid — even one row out of alignment reads as a slide error.
claims.quote: the digitalization trend the internet of things trend is not fully aligned with all the other trends

claims.claim: When using a color gradient to encode a scale (e.g., low-to-high impact), make the shade steps distinct enough to actually read as different values, not just position.
claims.quote: there could be a little bit more differences between the color shades here

claims.claim: To improve your own slide-writing, deliberately study strong examples (e.g., consulting-firm published exhibits) and name the specific tactics they use before applying them to your own work.
claims.quote: learn from the best observing the way people present

claims.claim: Keep every part of a slide body (everything except the title and footnotes) at one consistent font size — mixed sizes are a top cause of a slide looking messy.
claims.quote: the body of your slide, so everything except for the title and maybe some footnotes, should be the same font size

claims.claim: A single slide mixing seven-plus font sizes (28, 24, 20, 18, 12 in one example) is the concrete signature of an unorganized page.
claims.quote: the action title 28. Here this title, 24

claims.claim: Dotted lines in a chart should stay light and recede into the background — thick, dominant dotted lines look wrong and draw the eye to the wrong element.
claims.quote: usually if you make dotted lines, you don't want them to be so dominant

claims.claim: Any color used on a page must carry either an inherent, self-evident meaning or be explained with a legend — arbitrary color choices look unsophisticated.
claims.quote: whenever you use colors on your page, it either has a direct meaning or the needs to be legend

claims.claim: Elements (action titles, bullets, footers) that shift position between adjacent slides — jittering when you scroll a PDF — read as unaligned and unprofessional.
claims.quote: several elements are jittering, are moving

claims.claim: Check for page-to-page jitter across your whole deck (titles, bullets, footers) as a final polish pass — it's a quiet tell of unprofessional work.
claims.quote: make sure that you have no jarring on your pages

claims.claim: Add thin separator lines between grouped elements on an otherwise decent slide — their absence is often exactly what makes a page feel unfinished.
claims.quote: these separator lines that you could include between these elements to make it look a bit more organized

claims.claim: When a slide introduces a set of elements (e.g., a company's competitive advantages), give that group an explicit label or subtitle instead of making the reader infer the organizing principle from the action title alone.
claims.quote: what is the title, or the organizing principle, of these elements

claims.claim: Whenever you show a percentage or market share, always state percentage of what (units vs. dollars, etc.) — an unlabeled percentage leaves the metric ambiguous.
claims.quote: always add the percentage of what are you looking at

claims.claim: The action title — a full-sentence takeaway, not a topic label — is described as a fundamental piece of every slide presentation.
claims.quote: action title's our fundamental piece of every slide presentation

claims.claim: A slide titled with just a topic header (e.g., "Market and Industry") instead of an action title is the single clearest reason a reader can't tell what the slide's message is.
claims.quote: the clearest thing that is missing is the action title

claims.claim: Never copy-paste a chart straight from a source report into a professional deck; if you already have the underlying numbers, rebuild the chart natively — it will always look cleaner.
claims.quote: never just copy paste charts like that

claims.claim: Define the scope of an industry, market, or metric (e.g., what "the industry" or "user penetration" refers to) before showing sizing charts about it — undefined scope makes even correct data unreadable.
claims.quote: so much remains in the dark. So pains of the industry. What industry exactly are you talking about here

claims.claim: Deword dense slides: say as much as possible with as few words as possible, replacing full sentences with tight bullet fragments that preserve full meaning.
claims.quote: you usually wanna say as much as possible with as little words as possible

claims.claim: Worked example of dewording: cut "The value of this information depends on the trust within the network" down to the bullet "Information value depends on network trust."
claims.quote: Information value depends on network trust

claims.claim: Full-sentence, paragraph-style slides will not be read even when handed out as printed reports — audiences skip dense text regardless of delivery format.
claims.quote: this is just something that will not be read

claims.claim: A quick dewording trick: delete articles like "the" from bullet text to cut words without losing meaning.
claims.quote: delete articles like "the" to deword the page

claims.claim: Excess animation and decorative color drown out the actual message a slide is trying to communicate — use graphical flourishes very selectively.
claims.quote: so many animations, so many colors that do not really add much to the actual content

claims.claim: Animation is inappropriate for C-level presentations and will read as unprofessional — leading firms don't use it.
claims.quote: animations is just not the look and feel that you should go for for C level presentations

claims.claim: Many consulting/executive presentations are never delivered live — they're printed and handed out for a meeting, which is part of why they favor a static, non-animated style.
claims.quote: often these presentations are not even getting presented, but they're just printed out as documents

claims.claim: Banking's "football field" chart (valuation ranges across methods) is standard inside banking but is understood by essentially no outside audience — the presenter never found a client who could read one.
claims.quote: nobody understands this outside of banking

claims.claim: Banking decks tolerate far more on-slide text than consulting decks; in a consulting main deck, an equally text-heavy page would be relegated to the appendix/backup.
claims.quote: in most consulting contexts, pages like that would never go into the main deck

claims.claim: For communicating insights up to leadership in C-level or boardroom settings, the sparser consulting slide style is a more reliable choice than the denser banking style.
claims.quote: the consulting style probably will be a bit more successful for you

claims.claim: There is no single universal rulebook for slide presentations — treat these fixes as one practitioner's calibrated opinion, not law, and expect reasonable disagreement.
claims.quote: there is no such thing as the law of slide presentations

claims.theme: status updates to a busy stakeholder
claims.claim: When reporting back to someone juggling several concurrent workstreams, open the update with a recap of what's been happening in this thread before asking anything new.
claims.quote: first open with a recap

claims.theme: status updates to a busy stakeholder
claims.claim: Write recaps and explanations in plain language rather than the jargon or shorthand built up during deep work — the reader isn't holding the same context you are.
claims.quote: explain things very simply so that I can quickly ramp back up on exactly what we're working on

claims.theme: status updates to a busy stakeholder
claims.claim: Ask one question at a time in a status update instead of bundling three or four — a batch of simultaneous questions is heavily taxing to process.
claims.quote: ask one question at a time

claims.theme: status updates to a busy stakeholder
claims.claim: Every update or summary should end by stating the next action explicitly, so the recipient knows exactly what moves the work forward without re-deriving it.
claims.quote: end with the next action

claims.claim: Attach concrete evidence (e.g., screenshots of the working feature) to a change report instead of asking the reader to reproduce and verify it themselves.
claims.quote: the agent actually does all of that and provides me with some screenshots

claims.claim: A review report should include an explicit risk assessment so the reader knows how deeply they personally need to scrutinize it before trusting the summary.
claims.quote: this risk assessment is uh super helpful because it tells me how much I need to actually look into the code

claims.claim: When a stakeholder needs to choose between visual/design options, render the real candidates (e.g., a page of spinner variations) instead of describing them in words — decisions on concrete visuals happen faster and more confidently.
claims.quote: generate a just a simple HTML page with some options for spinners so that we can choose the best one

disagreements.topic: Whether McKinsey's own real-world exhibits meet the "action title" ideal that McKinsey-trained consultants teach

positions.position: A published McKinsey slide's title ("five major trends could change the packaging industry") is judged too descriptive — it states a topic, not a point of view or standout insight.
The consulting-taught standard is that every slide needs a true action title (a full-sentence takeaway); a topic-only header is called out as the clearest cause of an unreadable page.

disagreements.topic: How much on-slide text is acceptable

positions.position: Banking presentations tolerate and expect much denser text than consulting decks, where equally text-heavy pages would be moved to backup/appendix.

gaps: None of the three talks cover live verbal delivery — pacing, body language, vocal tone, handling live Q&A, or presenting on a video call — only static slide/document design and written status updates.
No guidance on how to open or close a live presentation, structure a narrative arc across many slides, or manage a room's attention over time.
No discussion of presenting data insights to non-expert, non-corporate audiences (e.g., customers, the general public) — the examples are all consulting/banking/university-project decks.
No metrics on how long a dewording pass should take, how many words per slide is 'too many,' or how to test whether a slide's message actually lands with a reader.

The agentic-workflow video's recap/one-question-at-a-time/next-action pattern is designed for a person supervising several AI agents, not for presenting insights to a human audience or client — it's unclear how directly that pattern transfers to stakeholder presentations rather than async status pings.
No coverage of remote/virtual presentation tools (screen share etiquette, slide-to-video pacing) or of presenting with data-heavy dashboards instead of static slides.
